title: CHAPTER 15: ADMINISTRATIVE & REVENUE REFORMS UNDER BRITISH RULE

items: Introduction (Why this Chapter Matters)

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Permanent Settlement (1793) introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa created a loyal class of Zamindars and fixed state demand permanently.
Ryotwari System (1820) devised by Thomas Munro and Alexander Read established direct settlement with individual cultivators (Ryots) in Madras and Bombay.
Mahalwari System (1822) formulated by Holt Mackenzie held village communities (Mahal) collectively responsible for revenue payment in North-West Provinces and Punjab.
Lord Cornwallis, known as the 'Father of Indian Civil Service', separated executive from judicial functions through the Cornwallis Code of 1793.
British judicial structure evolved through Warren Hastings' Diwani and Faujdari Adalats to a unified legal apparatus culminating in the Indian Penal Code of 1860.

blocks.content: After the Revolt of 1857, the British government realised that mere military power was not enough to control India. They needed a strong, systematic, and centralised administrative structure and a stable revenue system to ensure uninterrupted flow of wealth from India to Britain. Therefore, a series of administrative, constitutional, judicial, military, educational, and revenue reforms were introduced. These reforms were NOT meant for Indian welfare but for strengthening British rule. This chapter is extremely important for SSC because questions are repeatedly asked from land revenue systems, civil services, army reforms, education policies, and Government Acts.

The Revolt of 1857 exposed the weaknesses of the East India Company. As a result, the British Parliament passed the Government of India Act, 1858. This Act ended the Company’s rule and transferred all powers directly to the British Crown.

items:
1. Government of India Act, 1858 – Provisions Explained
    • The post of Secretary of State for India was created in Britain.
    • He was assisted by a Council of India consisting of 15 members.
    • The Governor-General of India was redesignated as the Viceroy.
    • All powers – civil, military, revenue – came under Crown control.
    • The British government assured non-interference in religious matters (only on paper).

blocks.content: After 1858, the administration of India became highly centralised. The Viceroy acted as the supreme authority and governed India on behalf of the British Crown. Though advisory councils existed, real power remained with British officials.
The Indian Civil Service was the backbone of British administration. It controlled law and order, revenue collection, justice, and general administration.

blocks.content: The Revolt of 1857 was largely a sepoy uprising. To prevent future rebellions, the British reorganised the Indian army.

items:
1. Key Army Reforms
    • Ratio of British to Indian soldiers increased (from 1:5 to 1:2).
    • Indians were excluded from artillery.
    • Recruitment focused on so-called ‘martial races’ like Sikhs, Gurkhas, Pathans.
    • Indian soldiers were deliberately divided on caste and regional lines.

blocks.content: The main object of British administrative and revenue reforms was to secure maximum collection of revenue to meet imperial expenditures and maintain control over Indian territories.
The British introduced a uniform judicial system to strengthen their control. Traditional Indian legal systems were replaced by codified laws.

1. Permanent Settlement (1793)
Permanent Settlement (1793)

blocks.content: Introduced by Lord Cornwallis, the Permanent Settlement was implemented in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. Under this system, zamindars were recognised as landowners and revenue was fixed permanently.

items:
• Created a loyal class of zamindars.
    • Revenue demand was fixed, even during famines.
    • Zamindars exploited peasants.
    • Peasants lost ownership rights.
    • Agricultural growth was hampered.

blocks.content: Introduced by Thomas Munro in Madras and Bombay Presidencies, this system established direct settlement between the government and the peasants (ryots).

items:
• Eliminated zamindars.
    • Revenue demand was very high.
    • Frequent assessments caused insecurity.
    • Peasants fell into debt and lost land.

blocks.content: The British introduced limited local self-government mainly to reduce administrative burden. Lord Ripon is known as the Father of Local Self-Government in India.

items: Under Permanent Settlement, the Company retained 10/11th of the collected revenue while the Zamindars kept 1/11th; failure to pay by the specified date invoked the 'Sunset Clause'.
Charter Act of 1853 ended the patronage of the Court of Directors and introduced open competitive examination for the Indian Civil Service.
Cornwallis Code of 1793 explicitly separated revenue administration from judicial administration.
Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to qualify for the Indian Civil Service in 1863.

blocks.content: British education policy aimed to create a class of Indians who were Indian by blood but English in taste, opinions, and intellect.

blocks.content: British policies converted India into a raw material supplier and market for British goods. Indian handicrafts were destroyed, leading to deindustrialisation.
Although British reforms created a modern administrative structure, their real impact was economic exploitation, rural poverty, social discontent, and the rise of Indian nationalism.
